Your Inference Request Will Become a Black Box: Confidential Inference for Cloud-based Large Language Models

Chung-ju Huang Affiliation: Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China    Huiqiang Zhao Affiliation: Tencent, Shenzhen, China    Yuanpeng He Affiliation: Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China    Lijian Li Affiliation: Macau university, China    Wenpin Jiao Affiliation: Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China    Zhi Jin Affiliation: Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China    Peixuan Chen Affiliation: Tencent, Shenzhen, China    Leye Wang Affiliation: Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China
Abstract

The increasing reliance on cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) exposes sensitive client data, such as prompts and responses, to potential privacy breaches by service providers. Existing approaches fail to ensure privacy, maintain model performance, and preserve computational efficiency simultaneously. To address this challenge, we propose Talaria, a confidential inference framework that partitions the LLM pipeline to protect client data without compromising the cloud’s model intellectual property or inference quality. Talaria executes sensitive, weight-independent operations within a client-controlled Confidential Virtual Machine (CVM) while offloading weight-dependent computations to the cloud GPUs. The interaction between these environments is secured by our Reversible Masked Outsourcing (ReMO) protocol, which uses a hybrid masking technique to reversibly obscure intermediate data before outsourcing computations. Extensive evaluations show that Talaria can defend against state-of-the-art token inference attacks, reducing token reconstruction accuracy from over 97.5% to an average of 1.34%, all while being a lossless mechanism that guarantees output identical to the original model without significantly decreasing efficiency and scalability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that ensures clients’ prompts and responses remain inaccessible to the cloud, while also preserving model privacy, performance, and efficiency.

1 Introduction

The widespread deployment of cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini 2.5 Comanici et al. (2025) and GPT 5 OpenAI (2025a), brings powerful capabilities but also an immediate privacy hazard. Client data, including prompts and model responses, often contains personal, financial, or health information and, when processed on cloud, are exposed to the service provider (Fig. 1) Gim et al. (2024); Lin et al. (2025a). This exposure has already chilled adoption across regulated sectors (e.g., JPMorgan, Citi, and Goldman Sachs restrictions Farrell (2023); Bushard (2023); healthcare cautions about HIPAA compliance Bruce (2023)), underscoring that data confidentiality becomes a deployment prerequisite for trust. Beyond market signals, regulators likewise now expect systematic risk assessments: GDPR generally requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (PIA) for high-risk processing, and authorities have enforced these obligations against LLM providers Wolford (2025). For example, ChatGPT was temporarily banned in Italy and later fined €15 million for training on personal data without an adequate legal basis Pollina and Armellini (2024). In parallel, U.S. FTC oversight is pushing PIA-like reviews for AI services Bissex (2025), and Quebec’s Law 25 makes PIAs mandatory with significant penalties LégisQuébec (2021). Consequently, any trustworthy cloud-based LLM solution must provide end-to-end safeguards for prompts (and responses) to demonstrate PIA compliance.

Challenges. While ensuring prompt-response confidentiality, the primary challenge is satisfying three conflicting requirements, often termed the “impossible trinity” Gim et al. (2024); Luo et al. (2024): ① Model Privacy, which requires safeguarding client data without compromising the confidentiality of cloud-hosted models; ② Model Performance, which requires output invariance, i.e., that new mechanisms do not alter the model’s outputs; ③ Model Efficiency, which requires that privacy mechanisms introduce only modest computational overhead. This paper aims to realize a confidential inference mechanism that prevents the cloud from obtaining the client’s prompt and response while balancing the impossible trinity of model privacy, performance, and efficiency.

Status Quo. Current approaches to private LLM inference uniformly fail to balance this trinity (Tbl. 1). Data-centric methods, including differential privacy Wu et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2025) and anonymization Chen et al. (2023); Zeng et al. (2024), compromise performance by altering inputs, which violates output invariance. Homomorphic encryption-based mechanisms Liu and Liu (2023); Huang et al. (2022) provide provable security, but the large computational overhead and the need to access model parameters limit their widespread application in LLMs. Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs) with GPU support have been proposed as a path forward, promising greater efficiency by leveraging secure hardware enclaves. While CVMs can effectively isolate the runtime environment, existing implementations remain vulnerable; they do not prevent leakage of model parameters and the response, thus failing to provide comprehensive privacy guarantees Gim et al. (2024).

Our Solution. To address these limitations, we propose Talaria 11 1 In Greek mythology, Hermes wore the winged sandals Talaria, which allowed him to travel freely between the divine realm and the mortal world. Our method enables client data to traverse securely and efficiently between secure and non-secure zones., a novel CVM-based confidential inference paradigm that protects client prompts and responses by balancing model privacy, performance, and efficiency. The difference between Talaria and the existing CVM-based methods is shown in Fig. 2. Talaria uniquely partitions the LLM inference pipeline: sensitive operations involving client data are executed within a secure, client-controlled cloud CVM, while computationally intensive, weight-dependent operations are offloaded to the public cloud GPU. This Confidential Partitioned Inference (CPI) interaction is secured by our novel Reversible Masked Outsourcing (ReMO) protocol, which provides two-way protection by preventing the cloud from seeing client data and the client from inferring model weights. Empirically, Talaria thwarts state-of-the-art attacks, reducing token reconstruction accuracy from over 97.5% to just 1.34%. It achieves this robust security losslessly–guaranteeing bit-for-bit identical output to the original model–while demonstrating superior efficiency over existing CVM-based secure inference methods.

Our Contributions. The contributions of our work can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that protects client’s prompts and responses in cloud-based LLM inference.

  • •

    Talaria provides strong data privacy protection while maintaining a balance between model privacy, performance, and efficiency.

2 Related Work

DP-based methods. Differential privacy Dwork (2006) offers an efficient way to protect client prompts by perturbing the inputs, but this often comes at the cost of performance. DP-based techniques inject noise into token distributions, embeddings, or use paraphrasing to obscure original inputs Wu et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2024); Hong et al. (2024); Lin et al. (2025b). While highly efficient and not requiring changes to the backend model, this noise injection inevitably creates a trade-off between privacy and performance, as it can degrade the quality of downstream tasks.

HE-based methods. Homomorphic Encryption, often used with secure multi-party computation, allows for direct computation on encrypted data, promising strong, provable security for LLM inference without degrading output quality Liu and Liu (2023); Huang et al. (2022). However, the practical application of these methods to large-scale cloud-based LLMs is hindered by two major obstacles: prohibitive computational overhead that violates efficiency, and the need for model access, which compromises the model confidentiality.

CVM-based methods. CVMs provide a hardware-based TEE to isolate client data, but practical implementation for LLMs remains challenging. The naive approach of running one full LLM instance per client CVM, while secure Hanzlik et al. (2021); Lee et al. (2019), is unscalable and economically impractical due to the immense memory requirements of LLMs. Hybrid solutions attempt to solve this by processing prompts inside the CVM while offloading token generation to the cloud Gim et al. (2024). This improves efficiency but critically undermines the security model: it violates model confidentiality by exposing the model to the client and compromises client privacy by revealing the plaintext response to the cloud provider.

3 Threat Model

We consider a typical two-party cloud inference setting with: a cloud provider holds LLMs, and a client holds privacy-sensitive prompts and receives model responses.

Cloud. Consistent with related work Gim et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2025), we assume the cloud provider operates under the honest-but-curious threat model. The cloud is honest as it is economically motivated to follow the inference protocol faithfully; its business model relies on customer trust, which would be destroyed by any detected malicious tampering Sharma and Chen (2021); Xue et al. (2018). Simultaneously, the cloud is curious, meaning it may leverage its extensive computational resources to analyze prompts and responses, aiming to reconstruct sensitive client information or user attributes via inversion attacks Luo et al. (2025); Qu et al. (2025).

Client. The client is also honest-but-curious: it adheres to the protocol to obtain inference results while attempting to learn the cloud’s proprietary parameters (e.g., reverse-engineering model weights) from any messages it legitimately receives.

Trusted Computing Base (CVM). Our security model is based on the availability of GPU-accelerated CVMs. This assumption is practical, as major cloud platforms like Amazon Web Services AWS (2025), Microsoft Azure Azure (2025), and Google Cloud Google (2025) already provide such offerings. The client can verify the integrity of a CVM through remote attestation. Once verified, the CVM is considered a trusted extension of the client, allowing them to form a single logical party and securely share secrets. The CVM’s runtime state is cryptographically isolated from the cloud; the provider cannot directly access plaintext data inside the CVM. While the cloud cannot read the CVM’s runtime data, it retains control over how the CVM is provisioned. Following industry practice Russinovich (2024); Martinez (2024), the provider may enforce a minimal, pre-approved software stack and capability set to reduce misuse and to narrow the attack surface (e.g., blocking privileged or abuse-prone instructions and interfaces Schwarz and Rossow (2024), or enforcing launch control policies that only allow signed enclave binaries Schwarz et al. (2020)). These controls prevent a curious client from turning the CVM into an oracle for model extraction or systems introspection, without granting the cloud visibility into the CVM’s plaintext.

Out of scope. Following standard CVM practice Gim et al. (2024); Hanzlik et al. (2021), we exclude microarchitectural and side-channel attacks, physical attacks, supply-chain compromises, and denial-of-service. We also do not consider a fully malicious cloud that arbitrarily deviates from the protocol (see Sec. Limitations for discussion).

4 Methodology

4.1 Design Insight

Talaria enables Confidential Partitioned Inference (CPI) by decoupling computations that require proprietary parameters from computations that touch client plaintext. Concretely, we partition the standard LLM layer into:

  • •

    Weighted (weight-dependent) decoding: linear projections and other ops that multiply by model weights WW.

  • •

    Structural (weight-free) decoding: normalization, attention-score/softmax, residuals, and sampling that do not require direct access to WW.

We run the first category on the cloud GPU (holding WW) and the second inside the CVM, preventing the cloud from learning client data and the client from learning WW (Fig. 3).

Notations.

We use E∈ℝn×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} for a layer’s intermediate embeddings (sequence length nn, hidden dimension dd), W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} for the relevant weight matrix, E^\hat{E} and O^\hat{O} for masked inputs/outputs, O=E​WO=EW for the true weighted result, and XX for tokens. We list all the notations in Appx. A.

4.2 System Overview

The confidential inference process of Talaria is shown in Fig. 4.

4.2.1 One-time setup.

The client remotely attests a CVM and establishes a secure channel. The provider loads the model on a public GPU. We then precompute a reusable restoration pool for later recovery (Sec. 4.4).

Model partitioning. Each layer is split so that linear ops (e.g., Q/K/V and output projections in attention; MLP projections) execute on the unprotected cloud GPU, while structural decoding ops execute inside the CVM.

Restoration pool preparation. The CVM generates a public base Mpub∈ℝm×dM_{\mathrm{pub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} with m<dm<d, sends it to the GPU, and receives Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\mathrm{pub}}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}W back. RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}} will let the CVM later undo outsourced multiplications without ever obtaining WW.

4.2.2 Iterative inference.

For each decoding step, the client’s prompt XX is decrypted inside the CVM and embedded to EE. Before outsourcing any weight multiplication, the CVM masks EE (Sec. 4.3), sends only the masked tensor to the unprotected GPU for weighted decoding, and then locally restores the exact plaintext result and proceeds with structural decoding. The private KV cache remains in the CVM. The process repeats until 𝖤𝖮𝖲\mathsf{EOS}; see pseudocode in Appx. B.1.

4.3 Reversible Masked Outsourcing (ReMO)

Naively outsourcing E​WEW reveals EE to the cloud. ReMO prevents this with a reversible additive mask. Given E∈ℝn×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the CVM samples a secret mask M∈ℝn×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and forms

E^=E+M.\hat{E}=E+M.

Only E^\hat{E} is sent to the GPU, which computes

O^=E^​W=E​W+M​W.\hat{O}=\hat{E}W=EW+MW.

To recover the true result O=E​WO=EW inside the CVM, we must subtract the restoration term R=M​WR=MW. The core challenge is that RR depends jointly on the CVM secret MM and the cloud secret WW. Our protocol ensures neither secret ever leaves its trust boundary while still enabling exact restoration.

Correctness (output invariance).

ReMO is algebraically lossless: after restoration (Sec. 4.4), the CVM obtains exactly O=E​WO=EW. Hence, under a fixed sampler, responses with and without Talaria are bitwise identical (validated in Sec. 6.4).

4.4 Hybrid Masking Protocol

Hybrid masking separates mask generation from mask application so that the CVM can compute R=M​WR=MW without WW and the cloud can process masked data without MM.

Public base (setup).

The CVM samples a public base Mpub∈ℝm×dM_{\mathrm{pub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}, m<dm<d, and sends it to the GPU. The GPU returns the pre-multiplied pool

Rpub≜Mpub​W,R_{\mathrm{pub}}\triangleq M_{\mathrm{pub}}W,

which the CVM stores locally. MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}} is non-sensitive; RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}} is safe to keep in the CVM because, with m<dm<d, it reveals an underdetermined sketch of WW (formalized in Sec. 5.2).

Ephemeral private mixing (per token).

For each decoding step with sequence length nn, the CVM samples a fresh, private Mpvt∈ℝn×mM_{\mathrm{pvt}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} (never leaves the CVM) and derives

M=Mpvt​Mpub.M=M_{\mathrm{pvt}}M_{\mathrm{pub}}.

It forms E^=E+M\hat{E}=E+M and outsources E^\hat{E}. After receiving O^=E^​W\hat{O}=\hat{E}W, the CVM restores the plaintext result using only local secrets:

O=O^−M​W=O^−Mpvt​Rpub.O\;=\;\hat{O}-MW\;=\;\hat{O}-M_{\mathrm{pvt}}R_{\mathrm{pub}}. (1)
Security hooks for later analysis.

Eq. (1) keeps MM and WW in separate trust boundaries, supporting:

  • •

    Data confidentiality (Sec. 5.1): Each token uses a fresh, full-space mask (instantiated via a pseudorandom generator (PRG) inside the CVM), matching Def. 1.Additive masking gives the quantitative bound in Thm. 1.

  • •

    Model confidentiality (Sec. 5.2): With m<dm<d, Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\mathrm{pub}}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}W leaves a nontrivial right-kernel, so recovering WW from (Mpub,Rpub)(M_{\mathrm{pub}},R_{\mathrm{pub}}) is information-theoretically impossible.

Practical notes.

RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}} is prepared once per operation WW and reused across tokens; MpvtM_{\mathrm{pvt}} is sampled per token to ensure freshness. The KV cache is private and persists only inside the CVM.

4.5 Security Challenge and Threat Focus

Outsourcing weighted decoding naively exposes EE to a cloud adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}, enabling prompt/response inversion X′←𝒜⁡(E)X^{\prime}\!\leftarrow\!\mathcal{A}(E) with X′≈XX^{\prime}\!\approx\!X. ReMO with hybrid masking removes this leakage by ensuring the GPU only ever sees masked tensors and never receives enough information to infer MM (or undo it), while the CVM never obtains WW.

5 Privacy Guarantee Analysis

5.1 Data Confidentiality

Adversary and domain. We protect client prompts and responses against an “honest-but-curious” cloud that may adaptively query the protocol and analyze all public transcripts. We treat intermediate embeddings E∈ℝn×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} under a fixed, deterministic quantization into a finite ring (e.g., ℤ2k\mathbb{Z}_{2^{k}}) so that masking and indistinguishability are defined over a finite domain. All results extend to reals via standard discretization arguments.

Mask generation and freshness. For each decoding step (per token), the CVM samples a fresh, ephemeral private matrix Mpvt∈ℝn×mM_{\mathrm{pvt}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} and forms an additive mask M=Mpvt​MpubM=M_{\mathrm{pvt}}M_{\mathrm{pub}} using a public base Mpub∈ℝm×dM_{\mathrm{pub}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} established during setup. The mask is applied entrywise: E^=E+M\hat{E}=E+M. Freshness (single-use) and full-space randomness ensure the masked distribution does not concentrate on any known low-dimensional subspace.

Definition 1 (Computational indistinguishability).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any PPT adversary with access to all public auxiliary information ZZ (including protocol transcripts and MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}}). For any two inputs E1,E2∈ℝn×dE_{1},E_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with corresponding masked versions E^1,E^2\hat{E}_{1},\hat{E}_{2}, the distinguishing advantage is

|Pr[𝒜(E^1,Z)=1]\displaystyle\bigl|\,\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{1},Z)=1] −Pr[𝒜(E^2,Z)=1]|\displaystyle-\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{2},Z)=1]\,\bigr|
≤ε⁡(κ,q),\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon(\kappa,q), (2)

where κ\kappa is the security parameter of PRG used to derive masks and qq is the number of masked samples observed. If ε\varepsilon is negligible in κ\kappa for any polynomially bounded qq, the scheme is privacy-preserving.

Instantiation in Talaria. Within the CVM, masks are derived from a PRG keyed by a secret seed of length κ\kappa; conditioned on ZZ, the mask distribution is computationally indistinguishable from uniform over the ring (Appx. B.2). Because a fresh mask is used per token, the cloud cannot correlate observations across steps to reduce uncertainty.

Quantitative information-theoretic bound. Beyond computational security, the masking admits an information-theoretic guarantee that depends only on signal magnitude versus mask range.

Theorem 1 (Information-theoretic bound).

Let e=vec⁡(E)∈ℝNe=\mathrm{vec}(E)\in\mathbb{R}^{N} with N=n​dN=nd. Suppose the mask has i.i.d. coordinates mi∼Unif[−λ/2,λ/2]m_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-\lambda/2,\lambda/2] and e^b=eb+m\hat{e}_{b}=e_{b}+m for b∈{1,2}b\in\{1,2\}. Then the optimal adversary (with unbounded computation) that observes e^\hat{e} satisfies

Pr⁡[correctly distinguish ​E1​ from ​E2∣e^]\displaystyle\Pr[\text{correctly distinguish }E_{1}\text{ from }E_{2}\mid\hat{e}]\
≤12+12​min⁡{‖e1−e2‖1λ, 1}.\displaystyle\leq\ \tfrac{1}{2}\ +\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,\min\!\left\{\frac{\|e_{1}-e_{2}\|_{1}}{\lambda},\,1\right\}. (3)

Implications for parameterization. The distinguishing advantage scales as (effective) signal over mask range. Choosing λ\lambda so that ‖e1−e2‖1/λ\|e_{1}-e_{2}\|_{1}/\lambda is negligible for inputs drawn from the task distribution makes the optimal success probability arbitrarily close to 1/21/2. Practically, one can upper-bound ‖e1−e2‖1\|e_{1}-e_{2}\|_{1} via sensitivity estimates of the embedding map and set λ\lambda with a safety margin to cover worst-case layers/tokens (Appx. B.3).

5.2 Model Confidentiality

Goal. Prevent a curious client from recovering proprietary weights W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.

Mathematical isolation. The client observes only the linearly transformed Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\mathrm{pub}}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}W with Mpub∈ℝm×dM_{\mathrm{pub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} and m<dm<d. Since rank⁡(Mpub)≤m<d\operatorname{rank}(M_{\mathrm{pub}})\leq m<d, the right null space is nontrivial, dim(ker⁡(Mpub))≥d−m>0\dim(\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}))\geq d-m>0, and

{W′:Mpub​W′=Rpub}=\displaystyle\{W^{\prime}\!:\,M_{\mathrm{pub}}W^{\prime}=R_{\mathrm{pub}}\}= (4)
W0+{\displaystyle W_{0}+\{ Z:each column of Z∈ker(Mpub)}.\displaystyle Z:\ \text{each column of }Z\in\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}})\}.

Thus the feasible set is an affine subspace of positive dimension (infinitely many candidates), making unique recovery of WW information-theoretically impossible. Here ker⁡(M)={v∈ℝd:M​v=0}\ker(M)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\,Mv=0\}.

System-level hardening. We enforce remote attestation of the CVM image and restrict its capabilities to the minimal Talaria logic: no debug hooks, no general linear-algebra toolkits exposing arbitrary solves, and no interfaces that could be repurposed to probe RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}} beyond its intended use. Attestation binds code and configuration to a hash verified by the cloud, preventing a curious client from modifying the CVM to mount offline model-recovery oracles. See Appx. B.4 for formal proofs.

6 Evaluations

6.1 Evaluation Setup

All evaluations are conducted on a cloud node with 8 Nvidia H800 with 80GB of memory, 10 AMD EPYC processor cores, and 6400 GB of system memory. We enable security features such as AMD SEV-SNP AMD (2023) and NVIDIA GPU CC Nvidia (2023) for evaluations that require confidential computing. Detailed evaluation setup (datasets, metrics, etc.) can be found in Appx. C.1.

Datasets and models. We evaluate Talaria on four diverse datasets: Midjourney prompts AI (2024), WikiText-2 Merity et al. (2017), Patient-notes Ha et al. (2022), and GPT-OSS20B-samples Morris (2025). To simulate our threat model, we use 20% of each dataset as private client prompts and allow the remaining 80% to be used for training attack models. Our experiments leverage models from the Llama3 (1B, 8B, 70B) Meta (2025) and Qwen3 (0.6B, 8B, 32B) Alibaba (2025) families. By default, we use Qwen3-8B for all evaluations unless stated otherwise.

Metrics. For protection evaluation, we use Token Reconstruction Accuracy (TRA) and Cosine Semantic Similarity (CSS). The higher the TRA and CSS, the higher the similarity between the two texts, which can reflect the higher accuracy of the token reconstruction attack. For efficiency evaluation, we use end-to-end latency and Time to First Token (TTFT).

Attacks. We validate our defense against three SOTA reconstruction attacks targeting intermediate data: TokenInfer Luo et al. (2025) (classification-based), TokenInv Qu et al. (2025) (optimization-based), and SentenceInv Gu et al. (2023) (generation-based). By default, we use TokenInfer for most evaluations. According to TokenInfer, the reconstruction performance decreases as the number of layers increases. Therefore, in order to maximize the attack effect, we use the outputs of the first attention layer as the attack object.

Baselines. We first use No Protection and Full Isolation as the baseline, where the former is normal unprotected cloud inference and the latter is where each client loads a copy of the complete LLM into CVM for inference. Then we also use two SOTA defense mechanisms as baselines: SPD Gim et al. (2024), Cape Wu et al. (2025).

6.2 Protection Evaluations

We assess data privacy protection along two dimensions: input prompts and output responses. To facilitate comparison of metrics, we set the maximum number of output tokens per request to 100. Additional evaluations can be found at Appx. C.2.

Comparison with baselines. We evaluate the protection performance of Talaria against several baselines, with results summarized in Tbl. 2. No Protection highlights the severe privacy risk, as an adversary can infer both prompts and responses with near-perfect accuracy (avg. TRA > 97.5% and avg. CSS > 0.95). This demonstrates that without protecting the intermediate data, the cloud can easily infer the private prompt and response. While existing methods like Cape offer limited mitigation, they remain largely vulnerable. Another baseline, SPD, effectively protects prompts by processing the prefill phase within the CVM. However, this approach has a critical flaw: it exposes confidential model weights to the client. Furthermore, SPD leaves the generated response completely unprotected, as intermediate data during the decoding phase is transmitted in plaintext, leading to similarly high attack success rates (avg. TRA: 97.51%, avg. CSS: 0.9509). In stark contrast, Talaria provides robust protection across the board. It slashes the average TRA for prompt inference from 97.56% to just 1.34% and for response inference from 97.51% to 1.25%. Similarly, CSS plummets from over 0.95 to under 0.47. These results demonstrate that Talaria effectively defends inference attacks, rendering the recovery of private tokens nearly impossible.

Different LLMs. To assess the generalizability of our approach, we evaluate Talaria across a diverse set of models with varying architectures and parameter scales. As shown in Tbl. 3, Talaria consistently delivers strong protection for both client prompts and model responses, demonstrating its robustness and broad applicability.

Different Attacks. To rigorously assess its security, we evaluate Talaria against three SOTA attacks: TokenInfer, TokenInv, and SentenceInv. Against TokenInfer, the most potent of the three, Talaria proves exceptionally effective, reducing the average TRA to a mere 1.16% and the average CSS to 0.48. Our approach is similarly successful in thwarting TokenInv. Furthermore, Talaria effectively defends against SentenceInv, a prompt-only reconstruction attack for which TRA is not an applicable metric. These results demonstrate that Talaria provides comprehensive protection against a diverse range of sophisticated attacks.

6.3 Efficiency Evaluations

Our evaluation setup includes 1 to 32 clients, each of whom randomly selects 10 prompts from the Midjourney dataset. For ease of comparison, we fix the number of output tokens to 100. Finally, we calculate the average efficiency metrics.

Number of clients. Full Isolation requires a separate LLM instance for each CVM. When the number of concurrent clients increases, the operating system and GPU driver must perform expensive context switches. Therefore, as shown in Fig. 5(a), the end-to-end latency curve of Full Isolation rises sharply with the number of clients. Compared with the SPD mechanism, Talaria achieves better scalability because the SPD mechanism needs to infer multiple virtual prompts simultaneously to protect client privacy, which increases the memory usage. Compared to these two CVM-based approaches, Talaria demonstrates superior scalability by maintaining lower end-to-end latency as the number of concurrent clients grows.

Size of model parameters. As model size grows, all methods exhibit increased end-to-end latency (Fig. 5(b)). Compared with Full Isolation and SPD, Talaria is less affected by the expansion of parameter scale. Intuitively, Talaria confines weight-free operations to the CVM and outsources weight-dependent multiplications efficiently, avoiding the per-client model duplication and heavy context switching costs that penalize Full Isolation, as well as the additional overheads present in SPD. Talaria maintains robust token generation speed under larger models, delivering lower latency growth than Full Isolation and SPD as parameter scale expands.

Number of input tokens. Fig. 5(c) shows the change of TTFT as the number of input tokens increases (64→\rightarrow256). TTFT increases for all methods, but the growth is particularly steep for Cape, whose core routine computes contextual logits for every input token. Unlike No Protection, the three CVM-based designs (Full Isolation, SPD, and Talaria) cannot amortize prefill via multi-client batching because each request must run inside an isolated CVM, which inherently raises TTFT as inputs lengthen. Even under this constraint, Talaria consistently delivers the lowest TTFT among secure baselines and exhibits the mildest growth with respect to input length, yielding a faster first token–especially for long prompts. Talaria preserves strong isolation while keeping prefill latency close to the practical minimum for CVM-based schemes, thus offering the fastest initial response among secure methods as input tokens scale.

6.4 Output Invariance Evaluations.

We assess whether Talaria preserves the exact functional behavior of the LLM by generating paired responses with and without Talaria under an identical decoding setup (same model, tokenizer, fixed random seed, and deterministic sampler). We then compare the paired outputs using TRA and CSS, which respectively measure token-level identity and semantic equivalence. As detailed in Tbl. 5, Talaria achieves TRA=100% and CSS=1.00 for each dataset, indicating bit-for-bit identical responses relative to No Protection. These results empirically validate the losslessness of ReMO and local restoration pipeline and confirm that Talaria preserves output quality without perturbation and then satisfies the performance of the “impossible trinity” by guaranteeing output invariance while adding privacy protection. Additional invariance evaluations can be found in Appx. C.3.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Talaria, a confidential inference framework for cloud-based LLMs by partitioning the inference pipeline and leveraging CVMs and the ReMO protocol. Empirically, Talaria cuts reconstruction success to near-negligible levels across models, datasets, and attacks, while preserving bit-for-bit outputs and competitive latency. To the best of our knowledge, the first to keep both prompts and responses confidentiality while balancing model privacy, performance, and efficiency.

Limitations

The limitations of this work mainly include the following two aspects:

Threat Scenario. We adopt the standard honest-but-curious setting: the cloud provider executes the protocol correctly but may analyze observed artifacts to infer private information. This assumption is reasonable for cloud LLM services because ① providers are economically and reputationally incentivized to follow deployed protocols, making arbitrary deviation unlikely in practice; ② confidential-computing primitives (e.g., CVM attestation and capability scoping) already constrain what either party can do while still enabling routine operations; and ③ it aligns with the dominant threat model used in prior confidential-inference work Gim et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2025) and in our system design. Under this setting, our guarantees are testable, and the resulting system remains practical to deploy at scale.

We do not defend against a fully malicious or compromised cloud provider that can arbitrarily deviate from the protocol (e.g., returning malformed messages or bypassing attested images). Defending against such adversaries would require stronger mechanisms (e.g., verifiable execution, runtime auditing, or side-channel–resilient defenses), which we leave to future work.

Partial model protection. Talaria does not attempt to hide the entire model implementation from the client. Instead, it prioritizes weight confidentiality: proprietary weight parameters remain on the cloud side, while weight-free operators (e.g., normalization, attention scoring/softmax, residual connections, and sampling) are executed within the CVM. This choice is deliberate and reasonable. In contemporary LLM stacks, the structure of these operators is largely standardized and often public, whereas the learned weight matrices encode the provider’s core intellectual property and present the primary model-extraction risk. By keeping all weight-dependent computations on the cloud provider’s hardware and exposing only weight-free control flow, the client may observe the computation pattern but not the parameters.

Moreover, visibility into non-weight operators does not enable parameter recovery under our protocol. The client observes at most a fixed, underdetermined sketch Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\text{pub}}=M_{\text{pub}}W with m<dm<d, leaving a non-trivial right kernel and thus infinitely many WW consistent with the observation; without additional side information, the true weights are non-identifiable. In contrast, fully obscuring every non-weight detail would require heavy obfuscation or cryptography, undermining our efficiency and output-invariance goals. Prioritizing weight confidentiality therefore strikes a practical balance among privacy, performance, and scalability, yielding bit-for-bit identical outputs while protecting the provider’s proprietary parameters.

B.2 Theoretical Analysis of Def. 1

This section provides a theoretical foundation for Def. 1, which establishes the privacy guarantee of Talaria based on the standard cryptographic concept of computational indistinguishability. This principle is a cornerstone of modern cryptography, used to formally define the security of primitives such as pseudorandom generators and encryption schemes.

The indistinguishability game. The notion of computational indistinguishability is captured via a security game between a challenger and a Probabilistic Polynomial-Time (PPT) adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

  1. 1.

    Setup: The game is defined over two probability distributions, 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} and 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}. The adversary, 𝒜\mathcal{A}, is aware of these two distributions.

  2. 2.

    Challenge: The challenger secretly flips a fair coin, choosing a bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. It then samples a value vv from the distribution 𝒟b\mathcal{D}_{b} (i.e., v∼𝒟bv\sim\mathcal{D}_{b}) and sends vv to the adversary.

  3. 3.

    Adversary’s Goal: Upon receiving vv, the adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} must guess the original bit bb. It outputs a guess, b′b^{\prime}.

The adversary wins the game if its guess is correct (b′=bb^{\prime}=b). An adversary with no information can do no better than guessing randomly, succeeding with a probability of 1/21/2. The advantage of an adversary is defined as how much better than random guessing it can perform.

Adv(𝒜)=|Pr[b′=b]−12|\text{Adv}(\mathcal{A})=\left|\Pr[b^{\prime}=b]-\frac{1}{2}\right|

The two distributions, 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} and 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, are said to be computationally indistinguishable if the advantage of any PPT adversary is negligible–that is, smaller than any inverse polynomial in the security parameter.

The formula presented in Def. 1 is an equivalent and widely used formulation of this concept. Let 𝒜⁡(v)\mathcal{A}(v) be the output of the adversary on input vv. We can normalize the adversary’s output to be either 0 or 1. Let’s say 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs 1 when it guesses the sample came from 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, and 0 otherwise. The probability of the adversary guessing correctly can be expanded as:

Pr[b′=b]\displaystyle\Pr[b^{\prime}=b] =Pr[b′=1∣b=1]Pr[b=1]\displaystyle=\Pr[b^{\prime}=1\mid b=1]\Pr[b=1]
=+Pr[b′=0∣b=0]Pr[b=0]\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad+\Pr[b^{\prime}=0\mid b=0]\Pr[b=0]
=12​(Pr⁡[𝒜⁡(v,Z)=1∣v∼𝒟1]CLOSE\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(\Pr[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1\mid v\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}]
OPEN=+Pr⁡[𝒜⁡(v,Z)=0∣v∼𝒟0])\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad+\Pr[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=0\mid v\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}]\Bigr)
=12(Prv∼𝒟1[𝒜(v,Z)=1]\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]
=+(1−Prv∼𝒟0[𝒜(v,Z)=1]))\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad+\bigl(1-\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]\bigr)\Bigr)

Now, we can substitute this into the advantage formula:

Adv​(𝒜)\displaystyle\text{Adv}(\mathcal{A}) =|12(Prv∼𝒟1[𝒜(v,Z)=1]\displaystyle=\Biggl|\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]
=+1−Prv∼𝒟0[𝒜(v,Z)=1])−12|\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad+1-\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]\Bigr)-\tfrac{1}{2}\Biggr|
=|12Prv∼𝒟1[𝒜(v,Z)=1]\displaystyle=\Biggl|\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]
=−12Prv∼𝒟0[𝒜(v,Z)=1]|\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad-\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]\Biggr|
=12|Prv∼𝒟1[𝒜(v,Z)=1]\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl|\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]
=−Prv∼𝒟0[𝒜(v,Z)=1]|\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\quad-\Pr_{v\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[\mathcal{A}(v,Z)=1]\Bigr|

The formula in Def. 1 is:

|Pr[𝒜(E^1,Z)=1]−Pr[𝒜(E^2,Z)=1]|<ϵ|\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{1},Z)=1]-\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{2},Z)=1]|<\epsilon

Here, E^1\hat{E}_{1} is a sample from the distribution of masked embeddings derived from input E1E_{1}, and E^2\hat{E}_{2} is a sample from the distribution derived from input E2E_{2}. This expression is exactly twice the adversary’s advantage. Since a negligible function multiplied by a constant remains negligible, this formulation is cryptographically equivalent. It directly measures the difference in the adversary’s behavior when presented with samples from the two worlds, which is the essence of distinguishability.

Instantiation for Talaria. In our setting, the two distributions correspond to masked embeddings:

  • •

    𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}: E^1=𝖬𝖺𝗌𝗄⁡(E1)\hat{E}_{1}=\mathsf{Mask}(E_{1}),

  • •

    𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}: E^2=𝖬𝖺𝗌𝗄⁡(E2)\hat{E}_{2}=\mathsf{Mask}(E_{2}),

where 𝖬𝖺𝗌𝗄⁡(⋅)\mathsf{Mask}(\cdot) is a randomized masking transformation applied to the intermediate embedding matrix EE. To ensure soundness, the mask must satisfy two conditions:

  1. 1.

    Freshness: A fresh independent mask is sampled for each instance (e.g., per token).

  2. 2.

    Full-rank randomness: The distribution of masks must not confine noise to a publicly known low-dimensional subspace. Otherwise, the adversary could project onto the orthogonal complement and recover information about EE exactly. To prevent this leakage, the mask must span the full ambient space, e.g., via additive pads sampled from a pseudorandom generator (PRG) over a fixed modulus or via two-sided linear masking with secret invertible matrices.

In all cases, masking is performed element-wise over a fixed ring (e.g., ℤ2k\mathbb{Z}_{2^{k}} after deterministic quantization of EE), so that arithmetic and indistinguishability are defined over a finite domain.

Security guarantee. Formally, Def. 1 states that for all PPT adversaries 𝒜\mathcal{A}, for any two inputs E1,E2E_{1},E_{2}, and for any public auxiliary information ZZ (including protocol transcripts and public parameters),

|Pr[𝒜(E^1,Z)=1]−Pr[𝒜(E^2,Z)=1]|≤ε(κ,q)\big|\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{1},Z)=1]-\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\hat{E}_{2},Z)=1]\big|\leq\varepsilon(\kappa,q)

where κ\kappa is the security parameter (e.g., PRG key length), qq is the number of masked samples observed by 𝒜\mathcal{A} (including adaptive/chosen-input interactions), and ε⁡(κ,q)\varepsilon(\kappa,q) is negligible in κ\kappa for any polynomially bounded qq.

This guarantee holds under the assumption that, conditioned on ZZ, the mask distribution is computationally indistinguishable from uniform over the chosen domain, i.e., masks are generated by a secure PRG keyed within the client’s trusted environment.

Interpretation. Intuitively, the masking acts like a one-time pad over the chosen ring: once an embedding EE is combined with fresh pseudorandom noise that spans the full space, the resulting E^\hat{E} leaks negligible information about EE. Therefore, even a PPT cloud adversary observing E^\hat{E} together with ZZ cannot distinguish whether the input embedding originated from E1E_{1} or E2E_{2} with non-negligible advantage. This formalizes the confidentiality guarantee of Talaria.

B.3 Theoretical Analysis of Thm. 1

This section provides a formal derivation for the information-theoretic security bound presented in Thm. 1. The theorem quantifies the maximum probability with which an adversary can distinguish between two inputs, E1E_{1} and E2E_{2}, given only their masked versions. The analysis is “information-theoretic” because the resulting bound does not depend on the adversary’s computational power, but only on the statistical properties of the data and the masking mechanism.

The core of the proof relies on bounding the total variation distance (DT​VD_{TV}) between the probability distributions of the two possible masked outputs. The adversary’s optimal advantage in any distinguishing task is directly related to this statistical distance.

Preliminaries. We consider a game between a challenger and an adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The challenger chooses one of two inputs, E1E_{1} or E2E_{2}, with equal probability (12\frac{1}{2}). It then applies the random masking mechanism to produce a masked output E^=Eb+M\hat{E}=E_{b}+M, where b∈{1,2}b\in\{1,2\} and MM is a random mask. The adversary observes E^\hat{E} and must guess the original bit bb.

The optimal adversary’s probability of guessing correctly is given by:

Pr⁡[𝒜​ succeeds]=12+12​DT​V​(PE^1,PE^2)\Pr[\mathcal{A}\text{ succeeds}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}D_{TV}(P_{\hat{E}_{1}},P_{\hat{E}_{2}})

where PE^1P_{\hat{E}_{1}} and PE^2P_{\hat{E}_{2}} are the probability distributions of the masked outputs corresponding to inputs E1E_{1} and E2E_{2}, respectively. The total variation distance for two continuous distributions with probability density functions (PDFs) p1​(x)p_{1}(x) and p2​(x)p_{2}(x) is defined as:

DT​V​(P1,P2)=12​∫−∞∞|p1​(x)−p2​(x)|​𝑑xD_{TV}(P_{1},P_{2})=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|p_{1}(x)-p_{2}(x)|\,dx

Our goal is to bound this distance for our additive masking scheme.

Derivation for a single dimension. To build intuition, let us first consider a single-dimensional case. Let the inputs be two scalars e1,e2∈ℝe_{1},e_{2}\in\mathbb{R}. The mask mm is a random variable. For analytical clarity, we model the mask as being drawn from a continuous uniform distribution over the range [−λ/2,λ/2][-\lambda/2,\lambda/2]. The PDF of the mask, pm​(z)p_{m}(z), is:

pm​(z)={1λif z∈[−λ/2,λ/2]0otherwisep_{m}(z)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\lambda}&\text{if }z\in[-\lambda/2,\lambda/2]\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

The adversary observes e^=eb+m\hat{e}=e_{b}+m. The PDF of the observed value e^\hat{e}, conditioned on the original input being e1e_{1} or e2e_{2}, is simply a shifted version of the mask’s PDF:

p1​(x)=pm​(x−e1)​and​p2​(x)=pm​(x−e2)p_{1}(x)=p_{m}(x-e_{1})\,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\,p_{2}(x)=p_{m}(x-e_{2})

We can now compute the total variation distance:

DT​V​(Pe^1,Pe^2)\displaystyle D_{TV}(P_{\hat{e}_{1}},P_{\hat{e}_{2}})
=12∫−∞∞\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |pm​(x−e1)−pm​(x−e2)|​d​x\displaystyle|p_{m}(x-e_{1})-p_{m}(x-e_{2})|\,dx

The functions pm​(x−e1)p_{m}(x-e_{1}) and pm​(x−e2)p_{m}(x-e_{2}) represent two rectangular windows of height 1/λ1/\lambda and width λ\lambda, centered at e1e_{1} and e2e_{2}. The integral computes half the area of the symmetric difference between these two windows.

The area of this symmetric difference is the sum of the areas of the two non-overlapping parts. Each of these parts has a width of |e1−e2||e_{1}-e_{2}| and a height of 1/λ1/\lambda, provided that |e1−e2|≤λ|e_{1}-e_{2}|\leq\lambda (i.e., the windows overlap). The total area of the symmetric difference is 2×|e1−e2|×1λ2\times|e_{1}-e_{2}|\times\frac{1}{\lambda}.

Substituting this into the DT​VD_{TV} formula:

DT​V​(Pe^1,Pe^2)\displaystyle D_{TV}(P_{\hat{e}_{1}},P_{\hat{e}_{2}}) =min⁡(12​(2⋅|e1−e2|λ),1)\displaystyle=\min\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(2\cdot\frac{|e_{1}-e_{2}|}{\lambda}\right),1\right)
=min⁡(|e1−e2|λ,1)\displaystyle=\min\left(\frac{|e_{1}-e_{2}|}{\lambda},1\right)

Thus if |e1−e2|≤λ|e_{1}-e_{2}|\leq\lambda, the distance scales linearly; if |e1−e2|>λ|e_{1}-e_{2}|>\lambda, the distributions are disjoint and DT​V=1D_{TV}=1.

Generalization to multiple dimensions. Now let E∈ℝn×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and vectorize it as 𝐞∈ℝN\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} with N=n​dN=nd. Assume that the mask MM has independent coordinates mi∼Unif[−λ/2,λ/2]m_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-\lambda/2,\lambda/2]. Then the masked outputs 𝐞^1\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1} and 𝐞^2\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2} are uniform over two NN-dimensional boxes of width λ\lambda but shifted by δ=𝐞1−𝐞2\delta=\mathbf{e}_{1}-\mathbf{e}_{2}. The total variation distance factorizes across coordinates:

DT​V​(P𝐞^1,P𝐞^2)=1−∏i=1Nmax⁡(1−|δi|λ, 0)D_{TV}(P_{\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}},P_{\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}})=1-\prod_{i=1}^{N}\max\!\left(1-\tfrac{|\delta_{i}|}{\lambda},\,0\right)

Using the inequality 1−∏i(1−ai)≤∑iai1-\prod_{i}(1-a_{i})\leq\sum_{i}a_{i} for ai∈[0,1]a_{i}\in[0,1], we obtain the upper bound:

DT​V​(P𝐞^1,P𝐞^2)≤min⁡(‖𝐞1−𝐞2‖1λ, 1)D_{TV}(P_{\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}},P_{\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}})\leq\min\!\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{e}_{1}-\mathbf{e}_{2}\|_{1}}{\lambda},\,1\right)

Thus, the adversary’s distinguishing advantage is controlled by the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance between the inputs relative to the masking range.

Final bound. Substituting into the adversary’s success probability yields:

Pr⁡[𝒜​ correctly distinguishes ​E1​ from ​E2∣E^]\displaystyle\Pr[\mathcal{A}\text{ correctly distinguishes }E_{1}\text{ from }E_{2}\mid\hat{E}]
≤12+12​min⁡(‖E1−E2‖1λ, 1)\displaystyle\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\min\!\left(\frac{\|E_{1}-E_{2}\|_{1}}{\lambda},\,1\right)

This establishes the bound stated in Thm. 1. The result shows that the privacy guarantee is strengthened by increasing the masking range λ\lambda, and that the adversary’s advantage over random guessing vanishes as λ\lambda grows.

Remark on assumptions. The above derivation holds under the assumption that the mask entries are independent uniform random variables. If the masking distribution is generated differently (e.g., via structured or low-rank randomness), the exact form of the bound must be adapted to that distribution. In that case, the same total variation framework applies, but one must analyze the overlap of the induced distributions accordingly.

B.4 Theoretical Analysis of Model Confidentiality

This section provides a formal analysis of the mathematical guarantees that underpin Talaria’s model confidentiality, as introduced in the main paper. The core principle is to prevent a curious client, who controls a CVM instance, from reverse-engineering the cloud’s proprietary model weights, WW. This protection is achieved by structuring the interaction between the CVM and the public GPU as an underdetermined system of linear equations, making the unique recovery of WW information-theoretically impossible.

Problem formulation. During the one-time setup phase, the CVM receives a transformed version of the weight matrix:

Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\mathrm{pub}}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}W

where Mpub∈ℝm×dM_{\mathrm{pub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} is a publicly generated base mask, Rpub∈ℝm×dR_{\mathrm{pub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} is the published sketch, and W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are the secret model weights. From the client’s perspective, MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}} and RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}} are known, while WW is unknown.

Analysis as a system of linear equations. The matrix equation above can be decomposed into dd independent systems of linear equations, one for each column of WW. Let wjw_{j} and rjr_{j} be the jj-th columns of WW and RpubR_{\mathrm{pub}}, respectively. For each column j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,\dots,d\}, we have the following system:

Mpub​wj=rjM_{\mathrm{pub}}w_{j}=r_{j}

In this system, the matrix MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}} is the coefficient matrix, wjw_{j} is the vector of dd unknown variables (the weights in that column), and rjr_{j} is the known result vector.

Underdetermined constraint. The protocol enforces m<dm<d, so each system Mpub​wj=rjM_{\mathrm{pub}}w_{j}=r_{j} is underdetermined. Since rank⁡(Mpub)≤m<d\mathrm{rank}(M_{\mathrm{pub}})\leq m<d, the null space is non-trivial, with

dim(ker⁡(Mpub))≥d−m>0\dim(\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}))\geq d-m>0

The notation ker⁡(Mpub)\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}) denotes the kernel (or null space) of a matrix MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}}, defined as

ker⁡(Mpub)={x∈ℝd:Mpub​x=0}\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}})=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:M_{\mathrm{pub}}x=0\}

It represents the set of directions that are invisible to MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}}. If ker⁡(Mpub)\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}) is non-trivial, then any solution to Mpub​x=bM_{\mathrm{pub}}x=b can be shifted by an element of ker⁡(Mpub)\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}) to produce another valid solution, yielding infinitely many possibilities.

Solution space. Each solution set has the affine form:

wj=wp+whw_{j}=w_{p}+w_{h}

where wpw_{p} is a particular solution (e.g., wp=Mpub+​rjw_{p}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}^{+}r_{j} with the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse), and wh∈ker⁡(Mpub)w_{h}\in\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}}). Thus, infinitely many candidate weight vectors are consistent with the observed data.

Proposition (Non-identifiability under no priors).

Let 𝒮j={wp+z:z∈ker⁡(Mpub)}\mathcal{S}_{j}=\{w_{p}+z:z\in\ker(M_{\mathrm{pub}})\} be the solution set for column wjw_{j}. If no auxiliary constraints on wjw_{j} are available (i.e., the admissible set is ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}), then |𝒮j|=∞|\mathcal{S}_{j}|=\infty and the true weight vector is not uniquely identifiable. Uniqueness may arise only if additional side information restricts 𝒮j\mathcal{S}_{j} to a singleton (e.g., sparsity, low-rank priors, quantization).

Protocol constraints.

To preserve confidentiality in practice, the following requirements are critical:

  1. 1.

    Fixed sketch per matrix. For each WW, the cloud publishes a single Rpub=Mpub​WR_{\mathrm{pub}}=M_{\mathrm{pub}}W with fixed MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}}. Re-issuing with linearly independent MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}} is disallowed, since stacking multiple sketches could collapse the null space.

  2. 2.

    CVM attestation and isolation. Although the CVM performs unmasking internally, the client cannot read intermediate tensors (E,O=E​W)(E,O=EW); otherwise, by collecting enough input–output pairs, the client could solve E​W=OEW=O and reconstruct WW. Talaria relies on cloud-based attestation and runtime isolation to prevent such leakage.

  3. 3.

    Independent masking. Distinct, untied weight matrices (e.g., WQ,WK,WV,WOW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V},W_{O}) must use independent masks MpubM_{\mathrm{pub}} to avoid cross-module linkability.

  4. 4.

    Domain specification. The analysis assumes real-valued arithmetic. If weights are represented in finite rings (e.g., ℤ2k\mathbb{Z}_{2^{k}}), rank and null-space properties must be verified in that algebraic domain.

Conclusion.

The dimensionality constraint m<dm<d guarantees that Mpub​WM_{\mathrm{pub}}W alone does not uniquely determine WW, ensuring non-identifiability under standard assumptions. Model confidentiality thus holds provided that (i) no additional independent sketches are revealed, (ii) clients cannot access intermediate tensors, and (iii) no strong structural priors on WW are externally available.

Appendix C Additional Evaluations

C.1 Detailed Evaluation Setup

C.1.1 Datasets

We use four representative datasets in our experiments:

  • •

    Midjourney prompts AI (2024) is a dataset containing 246,381 natural language prompts for text-to-image service.

  • •

    WikiText-2 Merity et al. (2017) contains over 100 million tokens extracted from high-quality, curated Wikipedia articles.

  • •

    Patient-notes Ha et al. (2022) is a dataset containing 40,000 patient note history portions.

  • •

    GPT-OSS20B-samples Morris (2025) dataset is a collection of 8,960,000 text samples generated from a version of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS20B model OpenAI (2025b).

C.1.2 Metrics

For defense evaluation, we use Token Reconstruction Accuracy (TRA) and Cosine Semantic Similarity (CSS). TRA is formally defined as 𝑇𝑅𝐴=1|𝒯t​g​t|​∑ti∈𝒯t​g​t𝕀⁡(t^i=ti)\mathit{TRA}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^{tgt}|}\sum_{t_{i}\in\mathcal{T}^{tgt}}\mathbb{I}(\hat{t}_{i}=t_{i}) where 𝕀\mathbb{I} is the indicator function, 𝒯t​g​t\mathcal{T}^{tgt} represents the set of target tokens, and t^i\hat{t}_{i} denotes the reconstructed token corresponding to tit_{i}. CSS first extracts semantic embeddings of both reconstructed and ground truth prompts using Sentence-BERT Federici (2022) and then calculates their cosine similarity. Based on the prior work Luo et al. (2025), a TRA greater than 40% is considered sufficient for plausible reconstruction. For efficiency evaluation, we use end-to-end latency and Time to First Token (TTFT). End-to-end latency measures the end-to-end time from when the client sends a prompt to when they receive the complete response. Time to first token measures the time from request arrival to the generation of the first output token.

C.1.3 Attacks

We validate our defense against three SOTA reconstruction attacks.

Classification-based attack. TokenInfer Luo et al. (2025) reconstructs private tokens by intercepting the intermediate embeddings exchanged between devices in a distributed LLM framework. The core of the attack relies on the discovery that these intermediate embeddings form distinct clusters corresponding to their input tokens. The adversary trains a classification model to map the intercepted embeddings back to their original tokens. The attack model is a multi-layer perceptron consisting of six layers. Layer normalization and ReLU activation functions are used between consecutive layers. The training epochs for the attack model are 10.

Optimization-based attack. TokenInv Qu et al. (2025) is divided into two stages: First, a constrained optimization phase is used to recover a continuous embedding that is a close approximation of the original prompt. Second, an adaptive discretization phase accurately converts this embedding back into discrete text tokens by using the activation data and semantic speculation from another LLM to improve accuracy and readability. The attack model is set as optimization learning rate to 0.1, constraint coefficient to 0.1, optimization iteration number to 1500, embedding-based candidate size to 10, and semantic-based candidate size to 10.

Generation-based attack. SentenceInv Gu et al. (2023) trains a decoder model using a publicly available dataset from the same domain as a private target dataset. The decoder learns to reconstruct the original text from its sentence embeddings, which are generated by a pre-trained language model like BERT Devlin et al. (2019). The adversary then uses this trained decoder on the private embeddings to reconstruct the original, sensitive sentences, revealing high-level semantic information. The attack model is an adversarial decoder, which inherits from the transformer architecture with 6 decoding layers and 8 heads. The decoder is trained for 100 epochs with cross-entropy loss, AdamW optimizer Loshchilov and Hutter (2019), and a learning rate of 1e-4.

C.1.4 Baselines

We use two SOTA representative defense mechanisms as baselines:

  • •

    SPD Gim et al. (2024) first confines the client’s prompt and private data to a CVM, while splitting the computational workload with the untrusted cloud LLM provider. Then SPD uses prompt obfuscation to generate multiple plausible but fake “virtual prompts” that are processed alongside the client’s real one, making it impossible for the provider to distinguish the authentic prompt from the fake ones. In the evaluations, we set the number of virtual prompts to 15.

  • •

    Cape Wu et al. (2025) protects client privacy by locally perturbing the original prompt on the client’s device before it is sent to the cloud. It uses a hybrid utility function that considers both the context and token similarity to find suitable replacement words. A bucketized sampling method is then used to efficiently select a replacement token, which ensures differential privacy while trying to maintain the prompt’s original meaning. We set the number of buckets to 50 and use Bert Devlin et al. (2019) to capture contextual information.

C.2 Additional Protection Evaluations

Different LLMs. We assess the scale-robustness of Talaria by evaluating four datasets–Midjourney, WikiText-2, Patient Notes, and GPT-samples–across language models with increasing parameter scale. For each model, we measure the effectiveness of TokenInfer attack using two metrics, TRA and CSS. As summarized in Tbl. 7, Talaria consistently suppresses reconstruction across all model sizes and datasets, and the magnitude of protection remains stable as model capacity grows, indicating that the defense is largely model-agnostic.

Different attacks. We evaluate Talaria against three SOTA reconstruction attacks on four datasets. As summarized in Tbl. 8, Talaria consistently depresses both indicators across all datasets and attack families. The relative protection remains stable even when attacks are tuned to their strongest published settings, suggesting that Talaria provides attack-agnostic robustness rather than overfitting to any single threat.

Different layers. We evaluate the protection performance of Talaria against token reconstruction attacks at different layers, and use TokenInfer to attack the outsourced inputs of different layers of Qwen3-8B. For consistent comparison, we report both TRA and CSS over the concatenated prompt–response sequence rather than treating them separately. As summarized in Tbl. 9, across Q/K/V projections and MLP blocks at layers 1, 5, and 10 of Qwen3-8B, Talaria consistently collapses TokenInfer’s success from near-perfect to negligible. Before defense, early layers leak the most (e.g., Layer-1: TRA≈\approx98-99%, CSS≈\approx0.93-0.95), and leakage naturally diminishes with depth (Layer-10: TRA≈\approx83-84%, CSS≈\approx0.82-0.83). After applying Talaria, all submodules converge to low, layer-insensitive residuals: defended TRA stays around 1.1-1.4% (best: 1.08–1.14%; worst: 1.43%), and CSS falls to 0.45-0.48. The protection is uniform across pathways (Q, K, V, MLP vary within little TRA at a given depth), indicating that hybrid masking plus partitioned execution neutralizes the principal layer-specific leakage channels rather than merely shifting them deeper. Talaria turns high pre-defense leakage at shallow layers into uniformly low, sub-2% TRA and ≤\leq0.48 CSS across layers and submodules, demonstrating robust protection.

C.3 Additional Invariance Evaluations

Tbl. 10 provides three prompts together with the corresponding responses generated with and without Talaria. To remove randomness, we fix the model, tokenizer, decoding policy, and random seed. In all cases, the outputs are identical, with green shading used to mark the one-to-one correspondence. These examples complement the quantitative metrics and demonstrate that Talaria’s reversible masking and local restoration preserve the model’s behavior exactly, rather than only ensuring semantic similarity. Taken together, the results in Tbl. 10 confirm that Talaria maintains deterministic outputs while adding privacy protection, highlighting its effectiveness as a lossless mechanism.
